video.title: Designing a data-science module: Projects, reproducibility and rubrics
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Salma - statistics lecturer, Cairo University (main character)
Dr Amina Bello - lecturer in education, Lagos
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: My final exam was all calculations. My best students got top marks, then in their first internship they could not decide which analysis a real question needed. I had taught the tools, not the judgement.
Today: how to align a statistics or data-science module, design real projects, require reproducible work, and grade it fairly with a rubric.
Biggs calls it constructive alignment. Write the learning outcomes first, using verbs like analyse and justify. Then choose activities that practise those verbs, and assessments that measure them.

The GAISE college report asks for real data and real questions. A good project starts from a question the student cares about, uses messy public data, and ends with a claim, its uncertainty, and its limits.
Here is one way to spend fourteen weeks: four on inference, four on modelling, two on causal questions, and four on a staged project with a proposal, a draft and a final report.

Require every submission to run from raw data to final figure with one command, in a notebook or script under version control. If a marker cannot rerun it, it is not finished. This also discourages copied results.

Share the rubric when you set the project, not when you grade it. Describe each level in words a student can act on, and give feedback on the draft. Hattie and Timperley show feedback works when it says where to go next.
Quick check! An outcome says students will justify the choice of a statistical model. The only assessment is a timed multiple choice test of formulas. Is this aligned?
No. Justify is the verb, and a formula test cannot see a justification. A short written defence of a model choice on real data would measure it.
In the app, open the histogram lab. Change the bin width on the same data and notice how the story changes. Use it to show students why every choice in an analysis must be justified.
Your turn. When should students first see the project rubric?
When the project is set. Remember: align outcomes, activities and assessment, use real projects, require reproducible work, and share the rubric early.
Try it this week: take your module's learning outcomes, underline each verb, and next to it write the assessment that measures it. Any verb with nothing beside it needs a new task.

checkpoints.prompt: An outcome says students will justify a model choice; the only assessment is a timed formula test. Aligned?

options.text: Yes, if the test is hard enough
No, the test can't see a justification

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: assess the verb in the outcome, here with a written defence on real data.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: alignment means the assessment measures the outcome's verb, and justify needs written reasoning.

checkpoints.prompt: When should students first see the project rubric?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a rubric shared early guides the work and makes draft feedback specific.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a rubric only teaches if students can use it while they work.
